cues.text: The Gospels of Matthew and Luke record that Jesus was born at Bethlehem in Judea to the Virgin Mary, betrothed to Joseph of the house of David, during the reign of Caesar Augustus.

Luke tells us there was no room for them at the inn, so the child was laid in a manger; an angel announced the birth to shepherds keeping watch nearby, and a multitude of the heavenly host praised God.
Matthew adds the visit of the Magi, wise men from the East who followed a star to adore the newborn king.
A Date Anchored in History, If Not Precisely
The AD/BC divide in the Western calendar comes from the sixth-century monk Dionysius Exiguus, who calculated the year of Christ's birth for purposes of dating Easter — and got it slightly wrong.
Most historians, reasoning from the biblical references to Herod the Great (who died in 4 BC) and to a Roman census, place the actual birth around 6 to 4 BC.

The Western Christian calendar eventually adopted Dionysius's dating system, although other Christian traditions have used different calendar eras; by the fourth century, Rome had established December 25 as the liturgical commemoration of the Nativity.

For the Catholic faith, this is not merely the birth of a great teacher but the moment the eternal Word of God took on human flesh, uniting divine and human natures in a single Person — the doctrine of the Incarnation that everything else in this timeline presupposes.

The Magi's journey from the East is read as a first sign that the Gospel would go out not to Israel alone but to every nation, a mission that begins in earnest at Pentecost, roughly three decades later.
